title: Photodynamic Biomaterials for Microphysiological Tissue Engineering
text:
Microphysiological systems (MPSs) provide researchers with a biologically relevant platform to probe
cellular behavior in a simplified setting. At their simplest, MPSs involve encapsulating cells or spheroids of cells
within a 3D matrix and observing their behavior. While MPSs are providing significant insight into biological
function, these simple systems fail to capture the complexity of biology. This proposal develops important
photochemical molecules to incorporate dynamic cues, both physical and biochemical, into material platforms
for MPSs, thereby enabling the study of biologically relevant processes in vitro.

title: TCR Targeting Antibodies for the Treatment of T cell Cancers
text:
Few treatment options are available for T cell cancers that affect ~100,000 patients worldwide each year. The
current proposal will generate a type of immunotherapy using new antibodies that specifically kill the T cell
cancers and retain enough healthy T cells to maintain a functioning immune system. This immunotherapy may
improve patient outcome and limit side effects associated with traditional chemotherapies.

title: Multi-omics approaches to lower the barriers to sustainable production of plant natural products with relevance to human health
text:
Plants produce a plethora of medicinally important natural products that have significant potential to improve
human health yet are often produced in low amounts, in complex mixtures, and/or cannot be produced in a
sustainable or economic manner. Omics technologies enable the discovery of the biosynthetic genes of plant
natural products which can then be employed in commercial production of medically relevant compounds. In this
project, we will use state-of-the-art omics technologies to efficiently discover genes responsible for the
biosynthesis of eight pharmacologically relevant compounds and utilize this knowledge to revitalize an old
technology, plant cell culture, to enable robust, sustainable production of these products.

title: The Role of GPNMB in Parkinson's Disease.
text:
Despite intensive research, the etiology leading to neuronal cell loss in Parkinson’s diseases (PD), Alzheimer’s
diseases and related dementias remains unknown. Genome wide association studies (GWAS) have identified
numerous sequence variants associated with the risk to develop sporadic PD, however, there is little insight
regarding which and how these risk variants mechanistically contribute to the development and progression of
PD, thus impeding the clinical use and the development of novel therapeutics based on these data. This proposal
aims to systematical identify and define the molecular and cellular mechanisms how GWAS-risk variants
contribute to the development and progression of neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Targeting the NKG2A Pathway in Alopecia Areata
text:
Alopecia areata (AA) is one of the main dermatological disorders. With this project, we will study
the mechanisms of the NKG2A pathway in AA and provide preclinical proof of concept for the
treatment of AA using mouse model.

title: Microbubble augmentation of immunotherapy in head and neck cancer
text:
Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma is a common cancer with persistently poor prognosis and strategies to
prolong patients’ survival are desperately needed. We aim to use stable microbubble cavitation to improve
response rates to neoadjuvant aPD1 therapy while also identifying imaging biomarkers useful for guiding
treatment prior to surgery. We expect this protocol to provide groundbreaking data that can be used to support
larger phase II/III trials in microbubble-augmented immunotherapy.

title: Strategy Trial of Personalized Immunomodulatory Therapy for HIV-related Cryptococcal Meningitis
text:
8. Project Narrative
This project aims to test in a randomized controlled trial a strategy of using immune therapy that is
individualized among persons with cryptococcal meningitis in comparison to standard antifungal
alone. The project will also assess the change in inflammation in cerebrospinal fluid with
personalized immunotherapy.

title: Cancer Biology Program (CBP)
text: CANCER BIOLOGY PROGRAM: ABSTRACT The overarching scientific goal of the Cancer Biology Program (CBP) at the University of Arizona Cancer Center (UACC) is to understand the basic biological processes that underlie cancer etiology and progression. Our goal is to use the knowledge we generate on these processes to identify new therapeutic targets and biomarkers and to establish interprogrammatic collaborations to bring them to the clinic. The Specific Aims of CBP are to: (1) elucidate the basic mechanisms that control tumor-relevant cell growth and proliferation; (2) identify etiologic mechanisms in cancer initiation and progression; and (3) determine how the tumor microenvironment influences progression, invasion, and metastasis. CBP is comprised of 52 Members in 16 departments and five colleges. CBP Members have made a significant impact on basic cancer mechanisms as evidenced by being the first to: (1) identify a quiescence switch in dormant cells; (2) find a link between fumarate hydratase and ferroptosis in kidney cancer; (3) demonstrate centrosome loss as a major driver of prostate cancer initiation; (4) decipher the underlying functional defects in cancer-specific Polβ mutations; (5) identify a role for TDP-43 in DNA repair and stress granules; (6) identify a link between the androgen receptor (AR) and integrin α6β1 in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer; (7) find a role for estrogen receptor in suppressing mechanical-driven invasion in breast cancer; and (8) decipher how Helicobacter pylori evades the immune system to initiate gastric cancer. Through interprogrammatic collaborations and hand-offs to the Clinical & Translational Oncology Program, CBP Members are translating their findings by designing new drugs to target the androgen receptor and glycogen synthetase kinase in prostate and colon cancer, respectively; testing new Fe+ chelating agents in kidney cancer; designing peptides to target EGFR and integrin α6β1 in breast and prostate cancer, respectively; evaluating miR130b as a new biomarker for gastric cancer; using organoid/immune cell co-cultures to design personalized combination therapies for pancreatic cancer; and testing cannabinoid receptor agonists to overcome bone pain in breast cancer patients. UACC provided support to CBP through funding of pilot awards and coordination of programmatic meetings, seminars, retreats, and workshops that foster intra- and interprogrammatic collaborations and transdisciplinary translational research. These meetings supported strategic recruitment of 17 new faculty since 2016. CBP has a peer-review funding base of $9.8M (direct costs) of which $2M (20%) is from the National Cancer Institute, $7.2M (73%) from other National Institutes of Health sources, and $0.6M (6%) from other peer-reviewed sources. This represents a 49% increase in peer-reviewed funding over the previous project period. During the current project period, Members authored 386 cancer-relevant publications, of which 46 (12%) were intraprogrammatic, 78 (20%) were interprogrammatic, and 187 (48%) were inter-institutional. In addition, CBP Members filed 29 patents, of which two were issued, and mentored over 50 trainees.

title: Center for Neural Circuits in Addiction
text:
Overall
Addiction is a chronic relapsing brain disorder, and understanding how the brain can go awry will speed the
design of more effective therapies. The University of Minnesota has thriving communities of both NIDA-supported
addiction researchers and biomedical technology innovators. By bringing these communities together, our
Center for Neural Circuits in Addiction drives innovative, high-impact research at the local and national level to
help curtail this growing health problem.

title: The relationship between neuronal activity and stroke
text:
Stroke is one of the leading causes of death and the leading cause of long-term disability in the USA,
and most of strokes originate from blood flow blockage known as ischemic stroke. This proposal seeks to
elucidate how the spread of evoked activity in cortex predicts the location and volume of stroke protection and
stroke damage in animal model of ischemic cortical stroke. We propose to apply a battery of the state-of-the-
art multimodal techniques that will enable detailed quantitative studies of our hypothesis, which has clear
translational potential.

title: Identifying metabolic targets to reinvigorate T cell exhaustion
text:
A major barrier limiting the durability of T cell responses in immunotherapy is the development of T cell
exhaustion or hyperresponsiveness. Rewiring of metabolic pathways is critical to appropriate T cell function,
yet the role of metabolism in T cell exhaustion is not fully understood yet. This study seeks to identify metabolic
mechanisms of T cell exhaustion, and whether they can be reversed to reinvigorate exhausted T cells.

title: State-dependent gating of memory and plasticity in the aging brain
text:
The overall goal of this research is to provide new insights into how sleep affects memory processing in the aging
brain. The long-term objective of this project is to understand how aging-related sleep disturbances contribute to
the memory problems seen in old age. Understanding how aging-related sleep disturbances cause neuronal
dysfunction may eventually lead to new therapeutic strategies to mitigate or prevent aging-related memory loss.

title: Computational Technology for Single-Cell Functional Genomics
text:
Genetic variants play a pivotal role in determining individual susceptibility to various diseases. This project
aims to elucidate the intricate roles of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in health and human diseases,
specifically their influence on cell-cell communication within tissue niches. By providing a deeper
understanding of these genetic regulators using functional genomics and computation approaches, the
research will potentially identify critical therapeutic targets of ligand-receptor pairs for future drug discovery for
genetic diseases.

title: In Vivo Gene Editing of B cells with NICE-AAV Vectors
text:
HIV-1 remains a substantial global health burden: antiretroviral therapy (ART) is capable of suppressing virus,
but not curing infected individuals. Although broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) are a highly promising
approach for cure, even the most potent molecules are currently only effective for a limited time period. Our goal
in this project is to develop an in vivo delivery approach that reprograms B cells to express bNAbs and similar
molecules for the lifetime of an individual, enabling long-term HIV-1 remission in the absence of ART.

title: Genome-wide structure-based analysis of protein-protein interactions and networks
text:
This project focuses on the incorporation of predicted three-dimensional structures of protein-protein complexes
into proteome-wide depictions of protein interaction networks. These structure-informed networks will be
organized into functionally meaningful clusters of groups of proteins including those that bind together to form
large complexes and those that work together in cell signaling pathways. This research program meets a grand
challenge in Systems Biology and will reveal mechanistic insights regarding fundamental cellular processes
underlying a range of human diseases.

title: Impact of Chlamydia-infected cells on non-infected bystander host cells
text:
Unlike in high-passage cell lines, low-passage cell lines exert cell-autonomous immune responses that are
better able to contain chlamydia infection—especially at low multiplicities of infection. The host factors and
pathways that are responsible for the enhanced containment are not defined but are host protein synthesis-
dependent and occur in the presence of non-infected neighbor (i.e., bystander) cells. The purpose of this
application is to use systems-level approaches to identify the immune and metabolic mechanisms that
Chlamydia-infected and bystander cells use to control chlamydia infection.

title: Project 3:  Identifying transcriptional driver genes and targeting transcription in TSC
text:
Project 3: Narrative 
In this project, we will examine the JUN-AXL pathway in TSC2/TSC1 deficient tumors, clarify how MITF/TFE 
transcription factors are regulated in TSC null cells and tumors, and study how renal organoids derived from 
TSC2 null induced pleuripotent stem cells (iPSC) are dependent on transcription factors. This research has 
relevance for all of the tumors that occur in TSC, including renal angiomyolipomas and 
lymphangioleiomyomatosis. In addition, this research has potential value for any cancer with TSC gene loss, 
which is about 2% of all adult cancers.

title: Novel animal models to dissect how lung macrophages contribute to SARS-CoV2 alveolar pathology and respiratory failure
text:
SARS-CoV2 is an ongoing global pandemic that targets the most vulnerable members of our society with
persistent, overwhelming inflammation of the lungs that can eventually cause respiratory failure and death.
However, the specific factors that act locally in the lungs to determine disease severity remain unknown. These
studies will contribute powerful new tools to obtain clinically relevant information about macrophages, the
predominant immune cells in SARS-CoV2 infection, including whether they prevent repair of lung damage during
infection, and whether they may be potential drug targets to reduce disease severity and death in humans
infected with SARS-CoV2.

title: Elucidating the Origins and Drivers of Clonal Dynamics in Hematopoiesis
text:
Blood diseases and cancer are often driven by the expansion of specific hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) clones,
a phenomenon also observed in aging, yet the mechanisms underlying these clonal dynamics remain poorly
understood. This project will develop scalable technologies to reconstruct HSC phylogenies and engineer mouse
models where individual cells record their lineage and signaling histories in their own DNA, enabling precise
measurement of clonal dynamics. By uncovering the factors that shape HSC populations over time, this work
will improve our understanding of aging, refine prognostic models for hematological diseases, and inform
therapeutic strategies.

title: Massachusetts AI and Technology Center for Connected Care in Aging and Alzheimer's Disease (MAITC)
text: ADMINISTRATIVE CORE: PROJECT SUMMARY Within the Massachusetts AI and Technology Center for Connected Care in Aging & Alzheimer's Disease (MassAITC), the Administrative (Admin) Core will provide strategic leadership, advanced operational infrastructure, and robust governance structures. It will administer the annual national competition for research projects in coordination with the AITCC, and foster strategic partnerships across the AITC Program to accelerate translation of technologies into real-world care settings. The MassAITC Admin Core will help to establish a robust pilot project research program and build an extensive network of technology researchers, stakeholders, and industry representatives working to develop, validate and deploy innovative technologies to support successful aging and care for patients with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and related dementias (ADRD). To accomplish these goals, this Admin Core will pursue three specific aims: (1) Provide strategic leadership and operational excellence through established governance structures that coordinate MassAITC activities and ensure alignment with AITCC priorities; (2) Administer the annual national competition for innovative research projects in coordination with the AITCC, leveraging our proven infrastructure to support pilot projects from solicitation through commercialization; and (3) foster strategic partnerships and facilitate collaboration across the AITC Program to accelerate translation of AI-enhanced technologies into real-world aging and AD/ADRD care settings. The Admin Core will maintain an Operations Committee comprising Center leadership with complementary expertise in machine learning, edge AI, sensor technologies, AD/ADRD bioinformatics, and clinical neurology to guide scientific direction and resource allocation. We will coordinate activities with the Research Innovation Core, track outcomes for AITCC reporting requirements, and maintain our public-facing website that has already reached 30,000+ viewers through educational webinars. The Admin Core will work closely with the AITCC to organize and implement the centralized solicitation and external review process while providing specialized support for pilot execution. Drawing on our demonstrated success supporting 53 pilots with 57% industry participation and 46% follow-on funding rates, we will leverage comprehensive pilot project administrative infrastructure to assist in managing an expanded pilot portfolio. Finally, the Admin Core will launch a National Network of Pilot Partners to accelerate pilot project research activities, coordinate MassAITC's engagement with the AITCC-led Stakeholder Engagement Team to ensure technologies are maximally adoptable by end users, and collaborate with the AITCC to develop themes, agendas, and logistics for the annual AITC Symposium.
